title: If Something Calls Your Name at Night, Don't Answer #shorts
description_hook: Grandparents in Korea and China still warn: the voice calling your name in the dark may not be a person.

lines.text: IF YOU HEAR YOUR NAME, DON'T ANSWER
lines.say: If you hear your name in the dark tonight, don't answer. Not yet.
lines.img: a teenage girl sitting up in bed in a dark apartment bedroom at night, staring at the half-open door to a pitch-black hallway, cold blue moonlight

lines.say: Rule two. Wait. A real person will call again. They say a spirit won't wait.
lines.img: a narrow apartment hallway at night lit only by a green exit sign, empty, the far end swallowed in darkness

lines.say: Rule three. In Korea, the reapers come in threes. They carry a list of names.
lines.img: three tall figures in long black coats and wide black hats standing under a flickering streetlight on a rainy city street, faces hidden in shadow

lines.say: Rule four. At funerals, families leave them three bowls of rice, straw sandals and coins.
lines.img: three small bowls of white rice, straw sandals and coins on a low wooden tray outside a gate at night, candlelight, drifting mist

lines.text: THE THIRD CALL IS MOM'S VOICE
lines.say: Rule five. The third call comes. It's your mother's voice, from the hallway.
lines.img: a dark bedroom door slightly open, a thin strip of warm light behind it, pale fingers curled around the edge of the door frame

lines.say: But your mother is asleep in the next room. So… don't answer.
lines.img: a woman sleeping peacefully in a dim bedroom, while through the half-open door behind her the hallway is completely black

loop_back: Rule five says to answer the third call, but the voice can't be Mom's — so the viewer is thrown back to rule one: don't answer.

gumi.say: Twice or three times, depends who you ask. Would you answer?

source: A widespread Korean and Chinese folk belief that spirits and reapers (jeoseung saja) call the living by name at night, and that answering lets them take your soul; versions differ on whether a spirit calls once, twice or three times. At traditional Korean funerals families set out saja-bap — three bowls of rice, straw sandals and coins — for the reapers.
